analysis.one_liner: Cuts carbon emissions through annually declining permit auctions, returning all proceeds as equal quarterly checks to households.
analysis.headline: A bill to cut U.S. carbon emissions 90% by 2050 and send the permit auction proceeds to American households as quarterly checks was introduced in December 2024 with no cosponsors and died in committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would require companies that sell oil, coal, and natural gas in the U.S. to buy a limited number of carbon permits at public auctions, with the number of permits shrinking each year until emissions are 90% below 2015 levels by 2050. Every dollar raised would be split equally among eligible residents as quarterly "Healthy Climate Dividend" checks, so most families would receive more money than the higher fuel prices cost them. It also adds fees on carbon-intensive imports like steel and cement so foreign producers can't undercut U.S. firms, funds pollution monitoring in communities hit hardest by fossil fuel emissions, and preserves citizens' right to sue oil companies over climate deception. The bill was introduced three weeks before Congress ended, referred to two committees, and never received a hearing, cosponsor, or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary households: the bill returns every dollar of permit auction revenue equally to eligible residents as quarterly tax-free dividend checks. Since a flat per-person payment exceeds what most low- and middle-income families pay in added energy costs, the majority of Americans would come out ahead financially while breathing cleaner air. Frontline communities near pollution sources would gain monitoring and enforceable co-pollutant protections, and U.S. manufacturers of steel, cement, and aluminum would gain border protection against unpriced foreign carbon.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low- and middle-income households via dividends

how_it_helps.text: Establishes a hard, declining cap on carbon emissions — starting 15% below 2015 levels and reaching 90% below by 2050 — enforced by requiring oil, gas, and coal companies to buy permits for every ton they sell.
Auctions the permits quarterly, starting at a minimum price of $40 per ton rising $10 per year, and deposits all proceeds into a Healthy Climate Trust Fund.
Splits the fund equally among eligible individuals as quarterly, tax-free Healthy Climate Dividend payments, so most households would receive more than their share of the added energy costs.
Adds border fees on carbon-intensive imports (steel, cement, aluminum, chemicals) so foreign producers cannot undercut U.S. firms paying for permits.

Directs air-quality monitoring and corrective regulation for frontline communities bearing disproportionate pollution, and preserves citizens' right to sue fossil fuel companies for climate-related deception and damages.

analysis.who_pays: Fossil fuel producers — oil, gas, and coal companies and importers — would pay for permits at a rising minimum price starting at $40 per ton, and would pass much of that cost to consumers through higher gasoline, heating, and electricity prices. Wealthier households and heavy energy users would pay more in fuel costs than they receive in dividends.
analysis.who_pays_short: Coal, oil, and gas producers and heavy fuel users

drawbacks.text: Requiring fossil fuel companies to buy permits would raise the price of gasoline, heating fuel, and electricity for consumers, at least until cleaner alternatives scale up.
Coal and oil-producing regions would bear concentrated economic losses as demand for their product declines, and the bill directs no dedicated transition aid to those workers or communities.
The bill sets a firm floor of $40 per ton of CO2 rising $10 per year, which is a substantial and escalating cost on energy producers that some economists would argue could be set more flexibly.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's main benefit is a binding, declining national cap on carbon emissions paired with dividends that would more than offset higher fuel prices for most households, since auction revenue is returned per person while costs scale with energy use. It also protects frontline communities and preserves climate lawsuits. The honest drawbacks are real: energy and consumer prices would rise across the economy, fossil-fuel-producing regions would bear concentrated job losses with no dedicated transition assistance, and the starting permit price of $40 per ton rising $10 per year is a firm, legislated price floor. Design choices like a hard cap, full dividend return, and border adjustments mitigate the usual carbon-tax regressivity, but the adjustment costs are real and the bill does not address them directly.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees on the day it was introduced, got no cosponsors, no hearing, and no vote, and died when the 118th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on December 16, 2024 — three weeks before the 118th Congress ended — and referred to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means Committees.
No representative signed on as a cosponsor.
No hearing, markup, or floor vote ever occurred; the bill's action history ends at committee referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fossil fuel producers, who would have paid billions annually for carbon permits, avoided that cost when the bill died; coal and oil communities also kept the status quo. Households never received the dividends.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil fuel producers avoided permit costs

against.name: Fossil fuel industry
against.what_they_did: Would have faced multibillion-dollar annual permit costs under the bill; the broader industry consistently opposed carbon pricing legislation of this kind, and no member of either party advanced it.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and never acted on it.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and never held a hearing or markup before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the bill had a single Democratic sponsor, zero cosponsors from either party, and never received a committee hearing.

industries.note: Coal would bear the highest effective permit costs under a cap shrinking to 10% of 2015 emissions by 2050, and the coal economy would shrink structurally. Communities dependent on it would lose jobs with no dedicated transition fund in the bill.

industries.industry: Oil and gas producers, refiners, and utilities
industries.note: These companies are the 'covered entities' required to buy permits for every ton of carbon in the fuels they sell, creating a new multi-billion-dollar annual cost. They would pass much of it to consumers as higher fuel prices, which is why their interest in killing the bill ran against the dividend the public would receive.
A rising carbon price makes wind, solar, batteries, and efficiency more competitive against fossil fuels, growing demand for these industries.
